analysis.one_liner: Bans capturing, importing, exporting, or breeding orcas, belugas, false killer whales, and pilot whales for public display.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the House; referred to two committees in July 2022, it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend two federal animal-welfare laws so that no new orcas, beluga whales, false killer whales, or pilot whales could be captured from the wild, imported, or bred in captivity for shows at marine parks. It would let NOAA refuse permits for capturing or importing these animals for display, ban exports except to sanctuaries or the wild, and make it illegal to breed them for public display. Animals already in tanks would stay where they are; the bill simply ends the supply of new ones.
analysis.who_benefits: Members of the public who oppose confining large, social whales in concrete tanks for entertainment, and the animals themselves. The bill's findings cite science that these species die prematurely and show signs of distress in captivity [S3]. Anyone who visits marine parks loses nothing they already see; existing animals could remain on display.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Captive whale welfare; park visitors' values

how_it_helps.text: Bars NOAA from issuing any permit to capture or import an orca, beluga whale, false killer whale, or pilot whale for public display, cutting off the removal of whales from the wild for shows [S2][S3].

Makes it unlawful to export these whales except to a marine mammal sanctuary approved as being in the animal's best interest, or for release to the wild, closing the option of shipping surplus animals to overseas parks [S3].

Makes breeding or artificially inseminating these species for future public display illegal under the Animal Welfare Act, meaning the captive population would phase out rather than be replenished [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Marine parks and aquariums that display these whales, which would lose their supply of new animals and eventually their headliner exhibits. There is no direct cost to taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: The bill does nothing for animals already in tanks; it prohibits capture, import, export, and breeding, but leaves existing cetaceans on display indefinitely [S2][S3].

Marine parks argue that public display funds rescue, research, and conservation work and gives millions of visitors a connection to these animals; ending the pipeline of new whales would wind down an attraction that supports those programs and park jobs.

The bill requires export only to sanctuaries or the wild, but true sanctuaries for orcas and belugas barely exist, which critics could note leaves few good destinations for animals parks no longer want [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is gradual and principled: no new whales would ever be taken from the wild or born into tanks for shows. The cost falls on a small industry that profits from displaying these animals, and on park audiences generations from now. The honest weakness is that the bill is a phase-out, not a rescue; it leaves today's captive animals in place.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to a subcommittee, but neither committee ever scheduled it for a hearing or markup, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Schiff introduced the bill on July 26, 2022 [S1][S5].
The Speaker referred it to both the Natural Resources Committee and the Agriculture Committee [S5].
On August 29, 2022, it was referred to the Agriculture Committee's Subcommittee on Livestock and Foreign Agriculture, and no further action was ever taken [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Marine parks that display these whales are better off: their ability to import, export, and breed new animals for shows was never restricted, and no park had to change how it operates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Marine parks, whose supply pipeline stayed open

for.name: Rep. Adam Schiff
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors.

for.name: 36 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; Chair David Scott (D-GA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 26, 2022, sent it to the Livestock and Foreign Agriculture Subcommittee on August 29, and never scheduled a hearing or markup.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; Chair Raúl Grijalva (D-AZ)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 26, 2022, and never scheduled the bill for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: All 37 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; because the bill never reached a floor vote, there is no roll call showing how the parties would have split.

industries.industry: Marine theme parks and aquariums (e.g., SeaWorld-style facilities)
industries.note: The bill would end the industry's supply of new orcas, belugas, false killer whales, and pilot whales by banning capture, import, export, and breeding for display, eventually eliminating the centerpiece exhibits these parks sell tickets to see. Parks can keep their current animals, so the loss is gradual rather than immediate.

industries.industry: Wild-capture operators and international cetacean traders
industries.note: The bill bars permits to take or import these whales for display and bans exports except to sanctuaries or release, cutting off the trade in wild-caught and captive-bred animals sold to parks.
